With reference to the results, as p-value < alpha, we will reject the null hypothesis and infer that there is a significant trend.

Performing Emerging Hotspot Analysis

The code below runs EHSA on the weekday–morning space-time cube to classify each hexagon into temporal hotspot/coldspot types.

set.seed(1234)

ehsa_weekend <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(
  x     = TRIPS_weekend_nb,   
  .var  = "TRIPS",     
  k     = 1,      
  nsim  = 99   
)

The code below attaches EHSA results back to the hexagon layer and keep only statistically significant cells for mapping.

ehsa_weekend_sf <- hexagon %>%
  select(HEX_ID) %>%
  left_join(ehsa_weekend, by = c("HEX_ID" = "location")) %>%
  filter(p_value < 0.1) %>%
  st_as_sf()

The code below applies the consistent legend order and color scheme to the data before plotting.

ehsa_weekend$classification   <- factor(ehsa_weekend$classification,   levels = ehsa_levels)
ehsa_weekend_sf$classification <- factor(ehsa_weekend_sf$classification, levels = ehsa_levels)

Distribution of EHSA Classes

ggplot(data = ehsa_weekend, 
       aes(x = classification, fill = classification)) +
  geom_bar(color = "black", alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ehsa_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of EHSA Classes – Weekend/Holiday (11am–8pm)",
    x = "EHSA Classification", 
    y = "Number of Hexagons"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )

st hexagons are classified as no pattern detected, indicating that weekend/holiday demand does not form stable clusters across much of the city. Among the significant classes, persistent coldspots and sporadic coldspots are the next most common, pointing to areas where trip counts are consistently low or intermittently low. Sporadic hotspots also appear in meaningful numbers, reflecting localized, irregular bursts of higher demand. In contrast, persistent hotspots are few, and consecutive hotspots/coldspots plus new hotspots/coldspots are rare, showing that newly emerging or sustained high-demand clusters are uncommon in this period. A small NA group reflects locations without enough information to classify.

Overall, the distribution suggests a spatially uneven weekend/holiday pattern dominated by low-demand clusters, punctuated by isolated, short-lived hotspots. This aligns with discretionary travel behavior: trips are less governed by routine commutes and more by ad-hoc activities, producing irregular surges at select nodes while most areas remain stably low.

EHSA map and Gi* Trends

# Create the EHSA map
tmap_mode("plot")
ehsa_map <- tm_shape(mpsz) + 
  tm_polygons(col = "grey90", border.col = "white") +
  tm_shape(ehsa_weekend_sf) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "classification",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = ehsa_colors),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "EHSA Classification",
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"))
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(mpsz_planning) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey30", lwd = 1.5) +
  tm_layout(
    main.title = "EHSA Map",
    main.title.size = 1.2,
    main.title.fontface = "bold"
  )

# Get one representative hexagon from each significant EHSA classification
representative_hexagons <- ehsa_weekend_sf %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(classification != "no pattern detected") %>%
  group_by(classification) %>%
  slice(1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(HEX_ID, classification)

# Extract Gi* trends for these hexagons
hex_trends <- gi_weekend %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(HEX_ID %in% representative_hexagons$HEX_ID) %>%
  select(HEX_ID, HOUR_OF_DAY, gi_star) %>%
  left_join(representative_hexagons, by = "HEX_ID")

# Create individual plots for each classification type
plot_list <- list()

for (class in unique(hex_trends$classification)) {
  hex_data <- hex_trends %>% filter(classification == class)
  hex_id <- unique(hex_data$HEX_ID)
  
  p <- ggplot(data = hex_data, aes(x = HOUR_OF_DAY, y = gi_star)) +
    geom_line(color = ehsa_colors[class], linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
    labs(
      title = paste0(class, "\n(", hex_id, ")"),
      x = "Hour of Day",
      y = "Gi*"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10, hjust = 0.5),
      axis.title = element_text(size = 9),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 8)
    )
  
  plot_list[[class]] <- p
}

# Combine trend plots
combined_trends <- wrap_plots(plot_list, ncol = 2) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Gi* Trends by EHSA Classification",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, hjust = 0.5)
    )
  )

# Convert tmap to grob
ehsa_map_grob <- tmap_grob(ehsa_map)

# Combine map and trends side by side
final_plot <- plot_grid(
  ehsa_map_grob,
  combined_trends,
  ncol = 2,
  rel_widths = c(1, 1),
  labels = NULL
)

# Add overall title
title <- ggdraw() + 
  draw_label(
    "Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) – Weekend/holiday (11am–8pm)",
    fontface = 'bold',
    size = 15,
    x = 0.5,
    hjust = 0.5
  )

# Combine title with plots
final_combined <- plot_grid(
  title,
  final_plot,
  ncol = 1,
  rel_heights = c(0.05, 0.95)
)

final_combined

The EHSA analysis reveals distinct spatial and temporal clustering patterns of weekend/holiday bus trips (11am-8pm), showing fundamentally different characteristics from weekday commuter patterns. The map (left) displays blue coldspots scattered across western, northern, and peripheral planning areas, indicating persistently low weekend trip generation in predominantly residential zones. Red and orange hotspots appear fragmented and dispersed across central, eastern, and selected northern regions, representing major recreational destinations, shopping districts, and tourist attractions. These hotspots are less concentrated than weekday patterns, reflecting leisure-driven rather than employment-driven travel dynamics.

The Gi* trend plots (right) demonstrate diverse temporal behaviors across classifications throughout the 11am-8pm window. Persistent hotspots (dark red, H0003) maintain strongly positive Gi* values (4-5), showing stable high-demand zones at major weekend destinations. Sporadic hotspots (orange, H0017 and H0010) exhibit fluctuating positive values, suggesting intermittent clustering as visitors arrive at leisure destinations at varying times throughout the day.

Persistent coldspots (dark blue, H0006) remain consistently negative (-0.5 to -1.0), confirming stable low-demand areas in residential zones lacking recreational attractions. Sporadic coldspots (light blue, H0468) show variable patterns, while new hotspots (pink, H0513) emerge with positive trends, representing areas developing high-demand patterns specifically during weekend leisure hours. Consecutive hotspots (red, H0110) maintain elevated Gi* values (4-5), indicating sustained demand at popular weekend destinations.

7 Conclusion

This study shows that Singapore’s bus demand is highly uneven across space and time, with three consistent signals. First, trip volumes are strongly right-skewed in every period: most hexagons generate modest activity while a small set of locations—typically major residential towns, transfer nodes, and mixed-use hubs—account for a disproportionate share of trips. Second, spatial autocorrelation is present but varies by period. Weekday mornings display the clearest and most contiguous clustering: high–high clusters align with large housing corridors feeding central employment areas, while peripheral/industrial belts form low–low clusters. Third, evening and weekend patterns are more fragmented. In the afternoon peak, high–high clusters shrink and disperse, and low–high outliers rise—evidence of transitional edges and mixed land-use environments as commuters spread across diverse destinations. On weekends/holidays, demand becomes leisure-oriented: persistent cold spots dominate many peripheral zones, while hotspots concentrate around retail, recreation, and tourist areas, often as sporadic rather than persistent classes.

Methodologically, the combined use of Local Moran’s I, Gi * , HCSA and EHSA provides complementary lenses: LISA highlights where similarity clusters and outliers sit; Gi* quantifies the intensity of local concentration; HCSA filters Gi* to statistically robust hot/cold spots; and EHSA adds a temporal dimension, distinguishing persistent, consecutive, new, and sporadic patterns. The Mann–Kendall test then probes whether within-period Gi* trajectories trend monotonically. Together, these tools reveal that persistent hotspots are relatively rare outside the weekday morning window; many high-demand areas behave sporadically or shift through the peak, and only a limited number of hexagons exhibit clear monotonic trends within the examined hours.

Planning implications follow directly. For weekday mornings, strengthening trunk capacity and feeder reliability in established high–high corridors is likely to yield the greatest benefit, while targeted coverage and frequency rationalisation may suit persistent low–low belts. Afternoon operations should emphasise flexibility: interlined routes, dynamic short-turns, or headway-based control can better accommodate the dispersed, heterogeneous pattern and elevated share of outliers. On weekends/holidays, service design should pivot toward destination-driven mobility—timed frequencies to malls, parks, waterfronts, and event hubs—while maintaining baseline coverage in stable cold-spot neighborhoods. Across all periods, monitoring sporadic hotspots identified by EHSA is critical for event-responsive capacity and passenger information.
